To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
people with autism fail to use information from the eye area of faces when making social judgements.
high-functioning adults on the autism spectrum fail to use the eye region of the face during emotion judgments, instead using the mouth region.
high-functioning individuals with autism fail to use information from the eyes when making emotion judgments from faces and instead rely on information from the mouths.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the nature and extent of the social cognitive deficits in autism.
the development and evaluation of new methods for the assessment and diagnosis of autism.
the nature of face perception in autism and how it relates to the social deficits seen in autism.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the results indicate an abnormal use of facial information during social judgments in high-functioning adults on the autism spectrum.
the findings of this study indicate that individuals with autism have an abnormal use of facial information.
the results of this study suggest that the abnormal use of facial information is related to gaze behavior in individuals with autism.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
individuals with autism are less likely to look at the eyes, and when they do look at the eyes they use the eye region less effectively than controls.
people with autism are impaired at making use of information in the eyes of faces, and that this is due to a tendency to look at mouths when viewing faces.
individuals with high-functioning autism are impaired in their ability to utilize facial information when making emotion judgments, and that this is due, at least in part, to a deficit in face gaze.
The main takeaway from our work is that
people with autism have difficulty using information from the eye-region of faces.
people with autism have a different strategy for processing information in faces.
people with autism are not impaired at using information from faces per se, but rather they fail to use information in faces in the way that is most useful to them.
